questions.q: A design specification
o: lists the requirements a product must meet
questions.why: It's written after research and used to evaluate.

questions.q: Anthropometrics is
o: the study of human body measurements for design
questions.why: Ergonomics uses this data.

questions.q: What is a design specification?
o: A sketch of the final idea
A list of measurable requirements the product must meet
questions.why: Each point should be testable in evaluation.

questions.q: Which research method gives primary data on how people actually use an existing product?
o: Observing users carrying out the task and recording the problems they meet
Looking up material properties in a data book
questions.why: Primary research is gathered first-hand. Watching real users reveals problems they may not mention. Reviews, data books and patents are secondary sources.

questions.q: What is meant by iterative design?
o: Producing one final drawing and making it
Repeated cycles of prototyping, testing and refining a design
questions.why: Iterative design improves a solution step by step, with each cycle of testing and evaluation informing the next version.

long.q: Write four specification points for a bedside lamp for children aged 5–8. Make each point specific and justify it; generic points such as 'it must be safe' score nothing.
scheme: B1: a specific safety point, justified, e.g. low-voltage LED with no hot surfaces, because children will touch it
B1: a measurable size or stability point, e.g. base at least 120 mm wide so it can't tip over on a bedside table
B1: a user point, e.g. a switch large enough for small hands and reachable from bed
B1: a cost, material or aesthetic point, justified, e.g. a stated maximum price; bright colours that appeal to the age group

questions.q: Which is a thermoplastic?
questions.why: Thermoplastics can be reheated and reshaped.

questions.q: A hardwood comes from
questions.why: e.g. oak, beech.

questions.q: An alloy is
o: a mixture of a metal with other elements
questions.why: e.g. brass (copper and zinc).

questions.q: Which property describes a material's ability to absorb energy and resist sudden impact without fracturing?
questions.why: Toughness is resistance to fracture under impact. Hardness is resistance to scratching and indentation, and a hard material can still be brittle.

questions.q: Why is a thermosetting plastic such as melamine-formaldehyde used for laminate kitchen worktop surfaces?
o: It can easily be reheated and remoulded
It is hard and heat-resistant, and does not soften when reheated
questions.why: Thermosets form permanent cross-links when cured, so they stay rigid and hard when heated. Remoulding on reheating is a property of thermoplastics.

long.q: Bicycle frames are often made from aluminium alloy rather than mild steel. Give two advantages and one disadvantage of aluminium alloy for this use.
scheme: B1: lower density, so the frame is lighter
B1: resists corrosion (protective oxide layer), so it won't rust
B1: a disadvantage, e.g. more expensive; harder to weld; lower fatigue strength

questions.q: Injection moulding is best suited to
o: mass production of identical plastic parts
questions.why: High setup cost, very low unit cost.

questions.q: A jig is used to
o: guide a tool so parts are made accurately and repeatably
questions.why: Useful in batch production.

questions.q: Which process makes many identical hollow plastic bottles?
questions.why: Injection moulding makes solid parts; vacuum forming makes thin shells.

questions.q: Which casting process is most suitable for a small, intricate silver jewellery piece?
questions.why: Investment casting reproduces fine detail from a wax pattern and suits small precious-metal parts. Sand casting gives coarse surfaces, die casting needs costly dies for volume, and slip casting is for ceramics.

questions.q: What is the purpose of annealing a metal?
o: To make it as hard as possible by quenching
To coat it with zinc to prevent rust
To give it a decorative chrome finish
To heat it so internal stresses are relieved and it becomes softer and easier to work
questions.why: Work-hardened metal becomes brittle; annealing restores ductility. Hardening, galvanising and plating are different treatments.

long.q: Compare injection moulding and vacuum forming for making 10 000 plastic phone cases.
scheme: B1: injection moulding: high mould cost but very low unit cost at volume
B1: produces precise, detailed, varied wall thickness
B1: vacuum forming: cheap moulds, but thin sheets and less detail
B1: judgement: injection moulding suits 10 000 units

questions.q: Designing for disassembly helps
o: recycling and repair at the end of a product's life
questions.why: Part of the circular economy.

questions.q: What does a life cycle assessment consider?
o: The environmental impact from raw materials to disposal
questions.why: Includes manufacture, transport, use and end of life.

questions.q: Which design choice makes a product easier to recycle?
o: Using a single material that is easy to separate
questions.why: Design for disassembly helps reuse and recycling.

questions.q: Which is an example of a closed-loop (circular economy) approach?
o: Sending products to landfill at the end of their life
A manufacturer takes back used products and recovers materials to make new ones
Burning products without recovering any energy
questions.why: In a closed loop, materials are kept in use by recovery and remanufacture instead of being discarded after one life.

questions.q: Why can a product with high embodied energy still be the more sustainable choice?
o: Because embodied energy does not affect sustainability
Because higher energy always means higher quality
Because it lasts much longer and replaces many short-lived alternatives over its life
Because it costs more to buy
questions.why: Life cycle assessment looks at the whole life: a durable product can have a lower total impact per year of use than several disposable ones.

long.q: Describe the stages of a life cycle assessment for a reusable stainless steel water bottle, and give one environmental impact at three different stages.
scheme: B1: stages named in order: raw materials, manufacture, distribution, use, end of life
B1: raw materials: mining iron ore, chromium and nickel uses energy and damages habitats
B1: manufacture: smelting and forming steel uses a lot of energy, giving CO₂ emissions
B1: another stage, e.g. use: washing uses water and energy; end of life: steel can be recycled repeatedly

questions.q: An exploded drawing shows
questions.why: Parts are drawn spaced along their assembly lines.

questions.q: Orthographic projection shows
o: front, side and plan views to scale
questions.why: Used for manufacturing drawings.

questions.q: What does third-angle orthographic projection show?
o: Front, plan and side views laid out with standard positions
questions.why: The plan goes above the front view in third angle.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a 3D CAD model over hand sketches at the development stage?
o: It can be rotated, modified and tested virtually, then exported for CAM or rendering
It needs no skill to produce
It is always faster for first ideas
It removes the need for a specification
questions.why: CAD models can be edited, analysed and sent straight to manufacture. Hand sketching is usually quicker for generating first ideas.

questions.q: A sectional view on an engineering drawing is used to
o: show the colour and texture of materials
show internal details by imagining the object cut through, with cut surfaces hatched
questions.why: Sections reveal hidden internal features clearly, with hatching on the cut faces, instead of relying on confusing hidden-detail lines.

long.q: In third-angle orthographic projection, where is the plan drawn, and where is the view from the right-hand side drawn? Sketch the layout of the three views and add the third-angle projection symbol.
scheme: B1: plan drawn directly above the front elevation
B1: view from the right drawn to the right of the front elevation
B1: correct symbol: the cone's side view on the left, its two circles on the right

questions.q: A potential divider with an LDR can be used to
o: switch on a light when it gets dark
questions.why: The LDR's resistance rises in the dark.

questions.q: A cam converts
questions.why: The follower rises and falls.

questions.q: In a control system, what is an input transducer?
o: A sensor that turns a physical change into an electrical signal
questions.why: For example a thermistor or light-dependent resistor.

questions.q: A potential divider has R1 = 10 kΩ at the top and R2 = 10 kΩ at the bottom, with a 6 V supply. What is the output voltage across R2?
questions.why: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) = 6 × 10 ÷ 20 = 3 V. With equal resistors, the supply is shared equally.

questions.q: In a control circuit, a transistor is often used to
o: act as a switch, letting a small input current control a larger current to an output device
store electrical charge for later use
questions.why: A sensor circuit gives only a small current; the transistor switches enough current to drive a motor, lamp or buzzer. Storing charge is a capacitor's job.

long.q: A driver gear with 20 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 60 teeth. The driver turns at 300 rpm. Calculate the gear ratio and the output speed, and state the direction the driven gear turns.
scheme: M1: gear ratio = driven ÷ driver = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 : 1
A1: output speed = 300 ÷ 3 = 100 rpm
B1: the driven gear turns in the opposite direction

questions.q: A design brief
o: is a short statement of the problem to be solved
questions.why: The specification comes after research.

questions.q: What should the evaluation of a design project do?
o: Test the product against the specification and suggest justified improvements
questions.why: Use evidence from tests and users.

questions.q: Why build and test models during development?
o: To check function, size and appearance before the final product
questions.why: Record what each model taught you.

questions.q: Which is the best way to generate a range of initial ideas?
o: Quickly sketch and annotate several different solutions before choosing one to develop
Draw one detailed idea in full colour
Copy the first product found online
questions.why: A range of annotated ideas shows creative thinking and lets the designer compare options against the specification before committing.

questions.q: Why should a folio record changes made during manufacture?
o: Because the product must exactly match the first idea
To hide mistakes from the examiner
To show problem-solving and explain why the final product differs from the plan
questions.why: Documented modifications show the designer responding to problems during making, which is evidence of real decision-making.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of CAD/CAM?
o: accurate, repeatable manufacture from digital designs
questions.why: Accuracy, speed and repeatability.

questions.q: What is meant by ergonomics?
o: Designing products to fit the people who use them
questions.why: Uses anthropometric data, such as hand sizes.

questions.q: What is planned obsolescence?
o: Making a product last for ever
Designing a product to have a limited useful life
questions.why: It raises sustainability concerns.

questions.q: Which is an example of inclusive design?
o: A luxury kettle made in a limited edition
A kettle designed for one celebrity client
A kettle with a large, easy-grip handle and a clear water gauge so that users with limited grip or sight can use it
A kettle with very small buttons to look sleek
questions.why: Inclusive design aims to make products usable by as wide a range of people as possible, including older and disabled users, without needing a special version.

questions.q: What does just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing aim to do?
o: Deliver materials and components only as they are needed, reducing the stock held
Store large stocks in case of shortages
Send all products by air freight
questions.why: JIT cuts storage costs and waste by matching supply closely to production, but it depends on reliable suppliers.

long.q: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of planned obsolescence for manufacturers, consumers and the environment. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: manufacturers: repeat sales and steadier income
B1: consumers: regular improvements and often lower initial prices
B1: consumers: replacing products sooner costs more; parts often can't be repaired
B1: environment: more waste (especially e-waste) and more resources and energy used
B1: a justified conclusion, e.g. referring to right-to-repair rules or designing for longevity

topics.name: A Level design and make project

questions.q: An A Level project evaluation should
o: test the product against the specification, with users
questions.why: Objective testing and user feedback.

questions.q: Why is a Gantt chart useful in a project?
o: It plans tasks against time so progress can be checked
questions.why: Update it as the project changes.

questions.q: What makes a client's feedback useful?
o: It is recorded and used to change the design
It is collected after the exam
questions.why: Show how each change came from evidence.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of interviewing the client at the start of an A Level project?
o: To ask them to design the product
To establish their needs, constraints and preferences, which shape the brief and specification
To agree the final colour only
To get their approval of the finished product
questions.why: Early client input defines the real problem, so the brief and specification are grounded in the user's needs rather than the designer's assumptions.

questions.q: Why should an A Level project include a risk assessment for the making stage?
o: To identify hazards and control measures so the product can be made safely
questions.why: A risk assessment identifies each hazard in the processes used and how it will be controlled, which is part of planning safe manufacture.
